title: Three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:1–15)
hook: Abraham runs to feed three strangers; Christians painted them as the Trinity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the God who sees: Hagar by a desert spring, naming God. Your line was thou god who seest me. Whose name did you learn? Day three hundred forty-nine.

A Russian icon, painted by a monk, is copied onto cards and walls in churches and homes far from Russia. Three figures with wings sit around a table. Their heads tilt toward one another. In the middle of the table there's a cup. The fourth side of the table, the side facing you, is empty, as if there's a place left open. The painter, a monk named Andrei Rublev, didn't invent the scene. The icon is known as the Trinity, but what it shows is a moment from Genesis: an old man's lunch with three strangers who showed up at noon.
screen: `THREE FIGURES AROUND A TABLE.` → `THE FOURTH SIDE IS OPEN.` → `A LUNCH FROM GENESIS.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent by the oaks of Mamre, in the Douay-Rheims, "in the very heat of the day." The worst hour to have guests. He looks up and sees three men standing nearby. And the old man doesn't wait. Genesis says "he ran to meet them from the door of his tent" and bowed to the ground. Second, the feast. He offers a little water and a morsel of bread, and then makes it much more. He hurries to Sarah: three measures of fine flour, make cakes. He runs to the herd for a tender calf. He brings butter and milk, and stands by them under the tree while they eat. A morsel turns into a banquet. Third, who they are. The text keeps shifting. Three men. Then the Lord speaks. Then two of them go on toward Sodom as angels. Genesis never explains it. Jewish tradition reads the three as angels sent by God. Some Christian writers, Ambrose and Augustine among them, saw a hint of the Trinity, which is what Rublev painted. And one visitor makes a promise: by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Behind the tent door, Sarah laughs. Fourth, what the Church took from it. The Letter to the Hebrews says not to forget hospitality, because some, by it, have entertained angels without knowing. Saint Benedict told his monks to welcome every guest as Christ himself. In Greek, hospitality is philoxenia: love of the stranger.
screen: `THE DOOR OF THE TENT, AT NOON.` · `A MORSEL BECOMES A FEAST.` · `THREE MEN, THE LORD, OR ANGELS?` · `WELCOME EVERY GUEST AS CHRIST.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer a guest something good. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next person likely to come through your door, or sit at your desk, or join your table. A friend, a delivery driver, a coworker, a child's friend after school. Now picture Abraham, running in the heat. What could you offer them that's a little more than a morsel? A real drink. A chair. Your full attention for five minutes. Something from the good shelf. Choose it now. If you pray, you can ask to see Christ in whoever comes. The bell holds the time.
Hospitality. Philoxenia in Greek, love of the stranger. Abraham running at noon to feed three visitors who turn out to carry God's promise.
Your line: strangers bring god. Today, when someone unexpected interrupts you, treat the interruption like a visitor at the tent door. Day three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Benedictine monasteries still follow Saint Benedict's rule to receive every guest as Christ, and Rublev's icon of the three visitors, often called the Trinity, is used for prayer by Catholics and Orthodox Christians alike.

fork.setup: you're Abraham, old now, resting at your tent door in the worst heat of the day. three strangers appear nearby. what do you do?

send a servant to ask their business.
fork.reveal: he runs, bows, and has Sarah bake cakes while he fetches a tender calf. the visitors carry a promise: a son by next year.

original.note: Greek: hospitality, literally love of the stranger. the word in Hebrews 13:2.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about being a good host.
what it means: an old man runs to welcome strangers at noon, and finds God's promise at his table.
what a scholar hears: the visitors shift between three men, the Lord and angels; Augustine and others saw the Trinity, and Rublev painted it.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 18:1–2 phrases quoted from memory ('in the very heat of the day'; 'he ran to meet them from the door of his tent'); confirm. The Douay-Rheims has 'the vale of Mambre' where the script says 'the oaks of Mamre' (Hebrew); confirm the choice.

Rublev's Old Testament Trinity, c. 1411–1425, in the Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow. 'About six hundred years old'. Confirm. The 'empty fourth side' is a common devotional observation, not a documented intention of the painter; phrased as 'as if'.
Augustine (De Trinitate II) and Ambrose read Mamre as a hint of the Trinity; Jewish tradition reads three angels. Confirm attribution.
Rule of Saint Benedict 53: all guests to be received as Christ. Paraphrased; confirm.
